summary: Discusses point-to-point and multi-endpoint topologies in RTP environments, and maps the central topologies common in video conferencing to RTP terminology.

eli5.summary: This shows the different ways video call participants can be connected, such as straight lines or through a middle point.

questions: how do video conferencing mixers and relays map to rtp
what is the difference between an rtp mixer and translator
what is a selective forwarding middlebox
what is an mcu in video conferencing
subtitle: A catalogue of the ways RTP endpoints, mixers, translators and conferencing boxes can be wired together.

tldr.problem: Terms such as MCU are common in the video conferencing industry but are not defined in RTP, which has led to confusion about how such devices should behave at the RTP and RTCP level.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names each topology (point to point, multicast, mesh, translators, mixers, selective forwarding middleboxes, MCUs and others) and describes how each handles RTP, RTCP and the media, plus the properties that differ between them.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational document that obsoletes RFC 5117 and adds topologies such as the Selective Forwarding Middlebox. It does not change what RFC 3550 specifies.

today: RFC 7667 is an Informational RFC. It obsoletes RFC 5117, and the unit metadata shows no newer RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not change what RFC 3550 specifies.

sections.title: Why RTP Topologies Need Names
sections.content:
RTP topologies describe how RTP entities are interconnected and how each handles RTP and its control protocol, RTCP. The RFC wants to clear up confusion around industry terms that RTP does not define, above all the Multipoint Control Unit (MCU).

In practice most multipoint conferences run through central units. An MCU may act as a mixer or a translator in RTP terms, and may add signaling and application features. The RFC focuses on the media transport side of those boxes.

This document replaces RFC 5117. It adds topologies that did not exist then, built around scalable video coding and simulcast, whose central unit is the Selective Forwarding Middlebox (SFM). It is informal and is not meant to update or change what RFC 3550 says. Each topology gets a shortcut name starting with Topo- so other documents can refer to it.
sections.eli5: Video calls can be wired in many ways, and people used the same words for different things. This document gives each wiring its own clear name.

sections.title: Translators Versus Mixers
sections.content:
Most of the middle boxes fall into two families. A translator turns each RTP stream it receives into a separate stream in the other domain and keeps the SSRC. A mixer may select one stream or combine several, but always sends under its own SSRC, optionally listing the sources in the CSRC field.

Translators come in two kinds. A Transport Translator changes only transport details such as addresses or packetization and leaves the RTP stream alone. A Media Translator changes the media itself, from removing parts of a stream to fully transcoding to another codec. Because a Media Translator changes what the receiver sees, it must rewrite RTCP receiver reports so that, for example, the extended highest sequence number makes sense for the stream it received.

A third variant is the back-to-back arrangement, where a middlebox joins two endpoints through two separate RTP sessions. There the middlebox can change SSRCs and CNAMEs freely, becomes responsible for congestion control on each side, and breaks the common view of the session.
sections.eli5: A translator is like an interpreter who repeats what each person says in another language and keeps their name tag. A mixer is like a host who blends what everyone says into one message under their own name.

sections.title: Direct, Multicast and Mesh Topologies
sections.content:
In Point to Point (Topo-Point-to-Point) two endpoints talk by unicast, which avoids the complexity of several parties. Any-Source Multicast (Topo-ASM) lets any group member send to everyone, so every member sees every RTCP feedback message and feedback suppression from AVPF is typically required.

With Source-Specific Multicast (Topo-SSM) only a Distribution Source can send to the group. Receivers send RTCP by unicast to a Feedback Target, as defined in RFC 5760. An extension in RFC 6285 lets a joining receiver catch up through a unicast session with a Burst/Retransmission Source.

In a mesh (Topo-Mesh) each endpoint sends to every other over separate unicast flows. These can form one joint RTP session, in which case the stream sent to everyone is the same and congestion control has to follow the most restricting path, or independent sessions per pair, where each can adapt separately but endpoints lose awareness of the other pairs and SSRC-based loop detection stops working.
sections.eli5: Everyone can shout into one big room, or one speaker can broadcast while the listeners whisper back to a helper, or everyone can call everyone else separately. Each way has its own pros and cons.

sections.title: Mixers, SFMs and MCUs
sections.content:
A Media-Mixing Mixer decodes the incoming streams, mixes them (audio mixing, or video tiling) and encodes a new stream. Its drawbacks are heavy processing, quality loss from re-encoding and added latency. A Media-Switching Mixer avoids decoding and encoding by forwarding the selected encoded stream under its own SSRC. It must rewrite the SSRC, the sequence number, the timestamp offset and sometimes the payload type, and a receiver switching sources needs a refresh point, which the Full Intra Request message can ask for.

The Selective Forwarding Middlebox projects every possible source into a per-endpoint independent session and chooses which sources actually send. It suits scalable video coding and simulcast and has very low delay, but endpoints need many decoder instances or fast decoder switching. It breaks RTP loop detection and makes SSRC values local to each leg.

The RFC also covers a video-switching MCU, which forwards a single selected stream and makes RTCP reports misleading, so it recommends a standard mixer instead. The RTCP-terminating MCU is described as very commonly deployed: each endpoint has its own point-to-point session with the MCU. Most deployed ones set the CSRC count to zero, so loop detection and active-speaker information are lost at the RTP level. A split component terminal uses separate subunits, for example for audio and video, that should share a CNAME so they can be synchronized. A mixer in one direction and a translator in the other (Topo-Asymmetric) is not recommended.
sections.eli5: A mixer blends everyone's voices into one. A forwarding box instead passes along the right person's video without touching it, which is quicker and keeps the quality.

sections.title: Comparing Topology Properties
sections.content:
The RFC compares topologies on a few properties. All-to-all transmission: the topologies closest to emulating Any-Source Multicast are the relay and the mesh with a joint session. Interoperability: translators, mixers, RTCP-terminating MCUs and mesh with individual sessions can change codec or transport. Per-domain bitrate adaptation: with ASM, SSM, joint mesh and relays, every sender must adapt to the weakest path, while translators, mixers, SFMs and MCUs let each domain adapt separately.

Aggregation of many streams into one helps endpoints with little receive capacity. Selection is almost always easy, while mixing costs more, and video tiling also lowers the pixel count per stream. Full session view and loop detection work when SSRC and CSRC identities are kept, as in ASM, SSM, joint mesh and relays. Back-to-back sessions, independent mesh sessions and SFMs break loop detection.

Section 5 of the RFC summarizes the result as a table that scores each topology as full, partial or no support for each property.
sections.eli5: Some setups let everyone hear everyone, some save bandwidth for people on slow connections, and some make it hard to spot a loop. The document is a scorecard for those trade-offs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mixers, SFMs and translators modify packets. That prevents end-to-end integrity and source authentication unless they are trusted devices inside the security context, for example able to send SRTP and SRTCP. If encryption is used, Media Translators, SFMs and mixers must be able to decrypt the media. A Transport Translator can work without the payload keys when it changes only unprotected parts such as IP addresses and UDP ports.

A device that is part of the security context and is subverted or misbehaving can mount serious attacks while participants believe the session is protected. Different domains can also be protected with different security strength, and the RFC advises negotiating similarly strong parameters in all domains. A mixer needs about one security association per domain, while a translator needs one per participant it translates towards. Group-based topologies such as ASM, SSM, relay and joint mesh need key management that supports groups and make source authentication harder.
sections.eli5: A box in the middle that changes your video must be allowed to open the sealed envelope. If that box is bad, it can fool everyone while they think the call is private.

viz.caption: HOW EACH MIDDLE BOX TREATS SSRC AND MEDIA

Own SSRC; CSRC may list contributors
Decodes, mixes or tiles, and re-encodes
Own SSRC; rewrites SSRC, sequence number, timestamp offset
Forwards the selected encoded stream, no decode or encode

viz.caption: PROPERTIES THE RFC USES TO COMPARE TOPOLOGIES

items.title: All-to-all media
items.text: Can everyone send to and receive from everyone else.

items.title: Interoperability
items.text: Can the box change codec or transport between domains.

items.title: Per-domain adaptation
items.text: Can each domain adapt its bitrate separately.

items.title: Aggregation
items.text: Can many streams be combined into one.

items.title: Loop detection
items.text: Can SSRC and CSRC reveal a media loop.
